title: Parthian Iran
subtitle: 148 BC – 224 AD · Nisa, Ecbatana and the Feudal Empire

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Arsacid Great Kings, the feudal confederacy, and the Kings of Persis

entries.label: Mithridates I — the conquest of Media and Persis
entries.hint: Building on his conquest of Media in 148 BC, Mithridates I took Persis and Babylonia, defeated a Seleucid counter-invasion and captured the king Demetrius II in 138 BC — transforming Parthia from a breakaway satrapy into the dominant power of the Iranian plateau within a single reign.
entries.note: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 36.1, 38.9 (the capture of Demetrius II).

entries.label: Mithridates II the Great — the height of the empire
entries.hint: Mithridates II extended Parthian authority from Armenia to the Indus, received the first recorded Parthian embassy from Han China, and was the first Arsacid king to take the old Achaemenid title 'King of Kings' on his coinage — the reign that set the pattern of a Parthia governing as a genuine imperial power, not merely a successful frontier kingdom.
entries.note: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, 123 (the Chinese mission of Zhang Qian's successors); Parthian royal coinage legends, c.109 BC onward.

entries.label: Orodes II — Carrhae and the wars with Rome begin
entries.hint: Orodes II's general Surena annihilated Crassus's legions at Carrhae in 53 BC, opening two and a half centuries of intermittent great-power war with Rome — even as Orodes, within his own court, had Surena executed soon after out of fear of his popularity, a telling instance of the crown's uneasy relationship with its own great noble houses.
entries.note: Plutarch, Life of Crassus 21–33; Cassius Dio, Roman History 40.12–27.

entries.label: Phraates IV to Vologases I — the long stand-off
entries.hint: Across five reigns Parthia and Rome settled into an uneasy equilibrium: Phraates IV returned Crassus's captured legionary standards to Augustus in 20 BC as a diplomatic settlement rather than a military defeat, and the two empires fought repeatedly over Armenia as a buffer without either achieving lasting conquest of the other's core territory.
entries.note: Res Gestae Divi Augusti 29 (the returned standards); Tacitus, Annals 6, 12–15 (the Armenian wars).

entries.label: Osroes I and the Trajanic war
entries.hint: Trajan's invasion captured Ctesiphon and briefly declared Parthia a Roman province in 116 AD, the deepest Roman penetration of the Iranian world in the empire's history — reversed within a year by revolt across the newly conquered territory and Trajan's own death, after which Hadrian abandoned the conquests entirely.

entries.label: Vologases IV to Artabanus IV — the sacks and the fall
entries.hint: Roman armies sacked Ctesiphon twice more, under Avidius Cassius in 165 and Septimius Severus in 197, each time withdrawing rather than holding the conquest — a pattern of Parthian resilience against Rome that contrasted starkly with the dynasty's final collapse from within, when the Persis vassal Ardashir defeated and killed Artabanus IV in 224.
entries.note: Cassius Dio, Roman History 71.2, 76.9; al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Ardashir's rebellion.

entries.label: The Great Houses — Suren, Karen and Mihran
entries.hint: Parthian kingship rested on a confederacy of seven great noble houses holding hereditary provincial power, military command and the right to crown the king — a structurally decentralised system, unlike Achaemenid or Seleucid central administration, that gave the empire resilience against outside conquest but chronic vulnerability to internal succession disputes.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 11.9.3 (on the Parthian council of nobles); Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.112 (naming the Surena house).

entries.label: The Kings of Persis — from Frataraka to Basileus
entries.hint: By the first century BC the frataraka of Persis had styled themselves outright kings (basileus) on their coinage while remaining Parthian vassals, continuing the fire-altar iconography and Achaemenid-echoing titulature their predecessors had begun under the Seleucids — the same local lineage and milieu from which Ardashir, the founder of the Sasanian dynasty, would eventually emerge.
entries.note: Kings of Persis coin series, British Museum; Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (2001 English ed.), on the Persis-to-Sasanian continuity.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Rome on the western frontier, the Kushans in the east, and Ardashir's rebellion

entries.label: The Capture of Demetrius II
entries.hint: The Seleucid king Demetrius II marched east to reverse Mithridates I's conquests but was defeated and captured, spending the rest of his life an honoured prisoner at the Parthian court — a humiliation that ended any realistic Seleucid hope of recovering Iran.

entries.label: The Battle of Carrhae
entries.hint: Surena's horse-archers and armoured cataphracts annihilated Crassus's seven legions near Carrhae, killing Crassus himself and capturing the legionary standards — the worst Roman military defeat since Cannae, and the battle that established Parthian cavalry tactics as a byword for danger in the Roman imagination.

entries.label: Mark Antony's Median Campaign
entries.hint: Mark Antony's invasion through Media Atropatene toward the Parthian heartland collapsed into a disastrous retreat after his siege train was destroyed, costing him a large fraction of his army — a defeat that, alongside Carrhae, cemented the Iranian plateau's reputation as unconquerable by direct Roman invasion.

entries.label: Trajan's Conquest and Withdrawal
entries.hint: Trajan's legions took Ctesiphon and reached the Persian Gulf in 116 AD, the furthest east Roman arms ever operated, before revolts across the newly conquered provinces and Trajan's death the following year forced a complete Roman withdrawal under Hadrian.

entries.label: The Eastern Frontier against the Kushans
entries.hint: On its eastern frontier Parthia contested control of Sistan and the approaches to Bactria with the rising Kushan Empire — a far less chronicled struggle than the Roman wars, but one that shaped the empire's eastern territorial limits for its entire existence.
entries.note: Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations (1st c. BC/AD, on the eastern provinces); Kushan and Indo-Parthian coin overlap evidence in Sistan.

entries.label: Ardashir's Rebellion and the Battle of Hormozdgan
entries.hint: Ardashir, a vassal ruler descended from the Kings of Persis, expanded his power across Fars before defeating and killing Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan on 28 April 224 — ending four centuries of Arsacid rule and founding the Sasanian dynasty that would govern Iran for the next four hundred years in turn.
entries.note: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings; the Sasanian royal inscriptions' own dynastic narrative (e.g. the Res Gestae Divi Saporis, retrospectively).
